RNA-C1.target: Explain emergence and persistence of internal RNA-poor cavities measured by arithmetic mean per-droplet hollow-area ratio f(t), with a mechanism prediction distinguishing composition-linked demixing from reaction-condition/carryover.
known_relations: f_A at 0,4,8,12,24 h = 0.01487, 0.00544, 0.00444, 0.00406, 0.00446; f_B = 0.01381, 0.01592, 0.02393, 0.04028, 0.08918 (initial_measurements.json). There are two independent preparations per condition; fields and objects are not independent preparation replicates.

C01: reference DNA read fraction 0.9466; four listed non-reference fractions sum 0.0500; full frequency sum is 0.9966. Repeat/rearrangement alignment is nonunique; DNA reads do not give RNA composition or active valence.
E02/fraction_dev: endpoint hollow-area means by template-length fraction are M near 0, M+L 0.04446, M+S 0.09412. These are not precise mixing ratios, RNA yields, or carryover-matched tests.

C04: phase partition ratios differ across tie-lines; reference K is about 239-525 on defined lines, variant K about 176-9032, while variant K on line 0 is undefined because dense and dilute concentrations are both zero. Error rectangles are not confidence intervals.
C03: tracking lacks persistent same-droplet cavity-area/state trajectories. C04 lacks phase volumes, time-resolved production/flux, and cavity-matched spatial concentrations.
C02 36/48 h values are descriptive, model-form-dependent extrapolations, not mechanism evidence.

hypotheses.statement: If transcription produces two RNA populations with different effective interaction valence, accumulation may cross a composition-dependent coexistence boundary inside an initially RNA-rich condensate. Selective partitioning could enrich one population in an outer dense phase and stabilize an internal RNA-poor phase, increasing hollow-area ratio after a local composition threshold. This proposed bridge couples composition-dependent internal demixing to selective partitioning; it is not inferred from DNA length or read frequency.
hypotheses.status_note: Untested. No supplied evidence establishes that a listed DNA variant changes RNA production, effective valence, cavity partitioning, internal coexistence, or image area.

hypotheses.statement: Amplification-associated carryover or another changed reaction condition alters transcription, ionic environment, or condensate organization without sequence composition mediating the hollow-area change.

gaps.description: No eligible literature result or supplied measurement provides a constitutive relation from RNA mixture composition and selective partitioning to onset or persistence of an internal cavity.
No matched time-resolved measurement connects template composition to transcribed RNA composition; DNA read frequencies cannot substitute for RNA concentrations.
No validated map connects f to phase volume, local concentration, or same-droplet cavity dynamics.

reply.summary: The supplied image statistic is the arithmetic mean of per-droplet hollow-area ratios f(t), not an area-weighted ratio and not a concentration. B rises from 0.01381 at 0 h to 0.08918 at 24 h while A falls from 0.01487 to about 0.004. Only two independent preparations per condition; fields and objects are not independent preparation replicates. C01 shows B DNA read heterogeneity (reference fraction 0.9466; listed other reads sum 0.0500; frequency total 0.9966), but repeated/rearranged sequence alignment is nonunique and DNA read fractions do not establish RNA composition or activity. C02 describes the observed trajectory but its extrapolations are model-dependent: B predicts f(36 h)=0.1207 and f(48 h)=0.1563 under rise-to-plateau versus 0.1239 and 0.1635 under a linear description; these are not mechanism evidence. E02/fraction_dev has M near zero, M+L about 0.0445, M+S about 0.0941 endpoint hollow-area fractions, but no precise mixture ratios, matched carryover, or RNA yields. C04 has species-specific phase partition ratios that vary by tie-line (reference K about 239-525 on defined lines; variant K about 176-9032), with variant K undefined on line 0 because both measured concentrations are zero. C04 lacks phase volumes, time-resolved yields/flux, cavity-matched concentrations, and a mapping from concentration to image area. C03 confirms no persistent same-droplet hollow-state/area trajectories. Proposed gap: the missing constitutive bridge from RNA mixture composition and selective phase partitioning to internal RNA-poor cavity nucleation and area fraction.

requests.model_spec: Use C04 phase_measurements.json. Variables: C_i^D and C_i^L in ng/uL; K_i=C_i^D/C_i^L dimensionless; x_V^L and x_V^D are variant mass fractions, dimensionless. For a closed two-species equilibrium mixture on one specified tie-line, x_V^D=K_V*x_V^L/[K_V*x_V^L+K_R*(1-x_V^L)]. Compare to the equal-partition alternative x_V^D=x_V^L. Evaluate x_V^L in [0,.01,.05,.10,.50,.90,.99,1], invert the mapping for hypothesized x_V^D thresholds [.1,.5,.9], compute conservative ratio rectangles using provided asymmetric errors and no statistical coverage claim. Do not pool tie-lines. Line 0 variant K is undefined because C_V^L=0. Check units, endpoint limits, equal-K identity, and all outputs in [0,1]. Conditions/assumptions: both RNA species present except at limiting endpoints; equilibrium, closed, two-species composition; K values are applicable to the mixture. These assumptions are unverified for cavities and the transcription reaction.

sources.title: RNA-driven phase transitions in biomolecular condensates.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: RNAs and RNA-binding proteins can undergo spontaneous or active condensation into phase-separated liquid-like droplets. These condensates are cellular hubs for various physiological processes, and their dysregulation leads to diseases. Although RNAs are core components of many cellular condensates, the underlying molecular determinants for the formation, regulation, and function of ribonucleoprotein condensates have largely been studied from a protein-centric perspective. Here, we highlight recent developments in ribonucleoprotein condensate biology with a particular emphasis on RNA-driven phase transitions. We also present emerging future directions that might shed light on the role of RNA condensates in spatiotemporal regulation of cellular processes and inspire bioengineering of RNA-based therapeutics.

sources.title: Chemically Informed Coarse-Graining of Electrostatic Forces in Charge-Rich Biomolecular Condensates.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Biomolecular condensates composed of highly charged biomolecules, such as DNA, RNA, chromatin, and nucleic-acid binding proteins, are ubiquitous in the cell nucleus. The biophysical properties of these charge-rich condensates are largely regulated by electrostatic interactions. Residue-resolution coarse-grained models that describe solvent and ions implicitly are widely used to gain mechanistic insights into the biophysical properties of condensates, offering transferability, computational efficiency, and accurate predictions for multiple systems. However, their predictive accuracy diminishes for charge-rich condensates due to the implicit treatment of solvent and ions. Here, we present Mpipi-Recharged, a residue-resolution coarse-grained model that improves the description of charge effects in biomolecular condensates containing disordered proteins, multidomain proteins, and/or disordered single-stranded RNAs. Mpipi-Recharged introduces a pair-specific asymmetric Yukawa electrostatic potential, informed by atomistic simulations. We show that this asymmetric coarse-graining of electrostatic forces captures intricate effects, such as charge blockiness, stoichiometry variations in complex coacervates, and modulation of salt concentration, without requiring explicit solvation. Mpipi-Recharged provides excellent agreement with experiments in predicting the phase behavior of highly charged condensates. Overall, Mpipi-Recharged improves the computational tools available to investigate the physicochemical mechanisms regulating biomolecular condensates, enhancing the scope of computer simulations in this field.

sources.title: Martini3-IDP: improved Martini 3 force field for disordered proteins.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Coarse-grained (CG) molecular dynamics (MD) is widely used for the efficient simulation of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). The Martini model, one of the most popular CG force fields in biomolecular simulation, was reported to yield too compact IDP conformations, limiting its applications. Addressing this, we optimized the bonded parameters based on fitting to reference simulations of a diverse set of IDPs at atomistic resolution, resulting in a Martini3-based disordered protein model coined Martini3-IDP. This model leads to expanded IDP conformations, greatly improving the reproduction of the experimentally measured radii of gyration. Moreover, contrary to ad-hoc fixes based on scaling of protein-protein or protein-water interactions, Martini3-IDP keeps the overall interaction balance underlying Martini 3. To validate that, we perform a comprehensive testing including full-length multidomain proteins, IDP-lipid membrane binding and IDP-small molecule binding, confirming its ability to successfully capture the complex interplay between disordered proteins and diverse biomolecular components. Finally, the recently emerging concept of biomolecular condensate, through liquid-liquid phase separation, was also reproduced by Martini3-IDP for a number of both homotypic and heterotypic systems. With the improved Martini3-IDP model, we expand the ability to simulate processes involving IDPs in complex environments, at spatio-temporal scales inaccessible with all-atom models.

sources.title: Interplay between charge distribution and DNA in shaping HP1 paralog phase separation and localization.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: The heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1) family is a crucial component of heterochromatin with diverse functions in gene regulation, cell cycle control, and cell differentiation. In humans, there are three paralogs, HP1α, HP1β, and HP1γ, which exhibit remarkable similarities in their domain architecture and sequence properties. Nevertheless, these paralogs display distinct behaviors in liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), a process linked to heterochromatin formation. Here, we employ a coarse-grained simulation framework to uncover the sequence features responsible for the observed differences in LLPS. We highlight the significance of the net charge and charge patterning along the sequence in governing paralog LLPS propensities. We also show that both highly conserved folded and less-conserved disordered domains contribute to the observed differences. Furthermore, we explore the potential co-localization of different HP1 paralogs in multicomponent assemblies and the impact of DNA on this process. Importantly, our study reveals that DNA can significantly reshape the stability of a minimal condensate formed by HP1 paralogs due to competitive interactions of HP1α with HP1β and HP1γ versus DNA. In conclusion, our work highlights the physicochemical nature of interactions that govern the distinct phase-separation behaviors of HP1 paralogs and provides a molecular framework for understanding their role in chromatin organization.

sources.title: Decoding phase separation of prion-like domains through data-driven scaling laws.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Proteins containing prion-like low complexity domains (PLDs) are common drivers of the formation of biomolecular condensates and are prone to misregulation due to amino acid mutations. Here, we exploit the accuracy of our residue-resolution coarse-grained model, Mpipi, to quantify the impact of amino acid mutations on the stability of 140 PLD mutants from six proteins (hnRNPA1, TDP43, FUS, EWSR1, RBM14, and TIA1). Our simulations reveal the existence of scaling laws that quantify the range of change in the critical solution temperature of PLDs as a function of the number and type of amino acid sequence mutations. These rules are consistent with the physicochemical properties of the mutations and extend across the entire family tested, suggesting that scaling laws can be used as tools to predict changes in the stability of PLD condensates. Our work offers a quantitative lens into how the emergent behavior of PLD solutions vary in response to physicochemical changes of single PLD molecules.
